On the first of every month a little drama was played in the small cottage of the old General and Madame B----. It came round as regularly as the month itself, and it always opened the same way, with Madame B---- standing at the bedside holding a cup of black coffee and waking the General.

On the first of the month the General had affairs to transact, and on mornings when affairs were to be transacted the household had little leisure. Honorine was the household, the whole of it.

On those mornings nobody saw the old dressing-gown, or the slippers, or the very old trousers, or the neck scarf knotted in a fashion that had been forgotten everywhere else for forty years. The General washed in warm water with a dash of cologne in it. Honorine trimmed his beard and his mustache. Then he put on a suit of black broadcloth and a stock of brown satin. He wore them with an easy, casual elegance that no one else could have, or could put on, as well as he did.

Nobody can say now whether the fine manners of the gentlemen of his day came naturally to them or were put on. Those gentlemen spent their youth in Paris getting manners and an education, came home with both, and never took either off again.

The first of the month was a holiday of sorts for Madame la Générale too. Old wives love to see their husbands dressed again in the manners and graces that won them when they were young. A woman wants to celebrate her conquest of her husband until the end of her life, and the worst thing that can happen to her is to watch the youthful husband turn old, ugly and commonplace. Under the gray hair and the wrinkles, old women still feel flutterings and thrills and strong emotions. The passions of a woman's heart go out only at death.

When Honorine brought the scissors to the white mustache and beard, her hands went cold, just as they had when she was sixteen. The lips under the mustache were still well formed and rosy, and when her fingertips brushed them she felt the touch on her own lips. The cologne was her secret delight. Buying it took the greatest economy she ever managed, a few sous held back here and there from every other expense. When she tipped it into the warm water she always felt a brief faintness, the same faintness she had felt as a bride coming out of the church on the General's arm. That was when she had first noticed the faint smell of a cologne bath. From one month to the next she looked forward to the thoughts that came to her in that moment.

The General had been a very handsome man. He belonged to a period that demanded physical beauty from Nature, and Nature always gives each period what it demands. If a period produces small men, or even gnomes and dwarfs, it is because the period asked Nature for them.

For the General, dressing was a ceremony, and he went through every part of it. When it was over he had his chocolate and his pain de Paris. Honorine could no more imagine him breakfasting on anything but pain de Paris than imagine him in a coat of some other color. After breakfast he settled into his large armchair at his writing desk to transact his affairs.

Pompey brought the mail.

"That idiot!" said the General. "That dolt! That sluggard, that snail of a Pompey! Not here yet! It is nine o'clock and I am ready. He should have been here long ago."

"But it is not nine o'clock yet, mon ami," Honorine called from the next room, where she was washing his cup, his saucer and his spoon.

"I tell you it is nine o'clock."

"Yes, yes, of course it is," she answered at once, and cheerfully. She always agreed with him at once, and always cheerfully.

"That Pompey gets worse every day. He is worthless, he is trifling. He ought to be discharged."

"Have patience, mon ami, a little patience."

Honorine had only one fault: she never learned from experience.

"Patience!" The General turned in his armchair. "Patience is an invention of dullards and sluggards. In a well-regulated world nobody would need it. Patience should be punished as a crime, or at least as a breach of the peace, and the police should look into it the way they look into smallpox. Patience! I never once heard that word in Paris. If a messenger in Paris asked anyone for patience, he would be beaten with a walking stick and told, 'We hire legs, not professors of patience!'"

"But, mon ami," Honorine said from the doorway, drying the spoon, "we don't pay Pompey. He fetches the mail out of kindness, to oblige us."

"Oblige! Kindness!" The General struck the desk with the flat of his hand. "A Black man oblige me? A Black man be kind to me? Favors, obliging, education, 'monsieur' this and 'madame' that. That is the new régime all over. And people call it a country! They call it a government! It is childish, madame. Childish."

Honorine put the spoon away and said nothing.

"And who knows what has been done to that mail before it ever reaches the box?" the General went on. "It has been tampered with, I have no doubt of it. The honesty of postal officials! A farce, madame, a farce from beginning to end." He drummed his fingers on the blotter, frowned at the clock, and settled the matter. "No, I'll tell you what it is. That Pompey went to the box and did not find the letter. That is the whole of it."

But he was not done. Every month, once he had finished with the post office, he turned abruptly to one more theory, and he turned to it now, lifting a finger as if Honorine had argued with him.

"And besides . . ."
